Javits Frimpong was shot and killed while walking to school in the Bronx. His death has sparked outrage in both Ghana and the US, and reignited debates about gun violence in America. "Javits deserved so much better and so do every single one of you," Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. "Though he was only a New Yorker for a short time, New York City will forever be proud to call Javits one of our own." Frimpong moved to the US about a year before the shooting. "I worked hard to bring you from Ghana to America because I wanted you to have opportunities, a better future, and a chance to achieve everything that you dreamed of," his father, Thomas Frimpong, said. His mother was granted an emergency visa from Ghana to mourn her son at Friday's funeral service, following Mamdani's lobbying of President Donald Trump earlier this month. stories.title: Sudan: West Kordofan - Intensified Conflict and Deadly Oil Pollution
stories.summary: Sudan: West Kordofan - Intensified Conflict and Deadly Oil Pollution Spesh531 / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0) A map showing the location of West Kordofan 20 November 2026 Ayin Network (Khartoum State) For nearly a decade, civil society groups in the oil-rich areas of West Kordofan State have raised environmental and health concerns linked to the oil sector, where local communities say industrial chemicals and petroleum residues, including oil leakages, have triggered an ongoing health crisis. The current conflict between the Sudan Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has compounded the problem further, especially now that it is flaring up in West Kordofan State, these local groups told Ayin. Since the war began, oil extraction facilities have been in the crosshairs of the warring parties. The destruction of pipelines, poor infrastructure maintenance, and lack of environmental oversight, local residents told Ayin, have only made conditions worse. "We have observed a severe deterioration in the situation since the war began," says one local civil society actor who has been documenting it. The source requested anonymity for security reasons. "There is no maintenance, and, in addition, there has been deliberate destruction, theft, and--in many areas--explosions at the oil wells," the source added.

stories.title: Africa: Africa Day At COP31 Calls for Water Security, Climate Resilience and Accessible Finance to Advance Agenda 2063
stories.summary: Africa Day At COP31 Calls for Water Security, Climate Resilience and Accessible Finance to Advance Agenda 2063 19 November 2026 Content from a Premium Partner African Development Bank (Abidjan) Africa Day at COP31 brought together African leaders, ministers, development partners, financial institutions, private sector representatives, civil society and youth representatives to advance a shared agenda on water security, climate resilience and climate finance. Held on 12th November in the margins of the Thirty-First Session of the Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) annual event, the high-level event was convened under the theme "Securing Africa's Water: Advancing Climate Resilience, Early Action and Climate Finance." Participants called for increased investment in water and sanitation as a foundation for resilience, sustainable development and economic transformation. The discussions underscored water's vital role in food systems, energy, public health, ecosystems, livelihoods and economic growth, while recognizing the growing risks posed by climate variability, droughts, floods and other extreme weather events. A severe drought that began in April has destroyed crops, while food brought in from elsewhere has become increasingly unaffordable. "Seven months without rain has brought us to this point where we now live in hunger," the 44-year-old farmer, who lives with his grandmother, wife and five children, told the BBC. "Even some of the wild plants that we used to eat have withered and dried up." Local officials say more than 90% of crops have failed in the region, where agriculture is largely rain-fed. Further south, in Malawi, Mathews Nkhambala has experienced the devastating effects of flooding. In April 2024, barely a year after Tropical Cyclone Freddy devastated the country's southern region, floods displaced people in Chikwawa district. The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country. In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.

stories.title: Town rebuilt after devastating floods becomes showcase for Libyan strongman's rule
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Whole areas of Derna have been entirely rebuilt By Tim Whewell Reporting from Derna Published 16 November 2026 "It was joy when I moved in. I could finally relax," says Abdulwahab Damdoum, surveying his luxurious new apartment overlooking the Mediterranean Sea, in the eastern Libyan city of Derna. Just three years ago he was clinging in terror to the roof of a house as the world's deadliest flood this century surged around him. Now the 27-year-old port worker, his wife and two young daughters have been given a new, free, 300-sq-m home in a showcase development commissioned by a son of Khalifa Haftar, the warlord who controls eastern Libya. It is part of a rapid $2bn (Â£1.5bn) rebuilding of Derna that the powerful Haftar family hope will serve as a model for development throughout Libya, increasing their influence across a country currently split between east and west, with rival governments in charge.
